chapter_theme: Poems 161-180 are almost all about giving and asking: Perunchiththiranar's and Saththanar's pleas to Kumanan and his gift of his own head, a bard's elephant tied in rebuke to a mean patron's tree, the hill chief Pittankotran praised by five poets as giver and as an anvil to his foes, the hunger-healer Pannan, and soldiers and small chiefs whose scars and spears feed the bards, with one brahmin sacrificer praised as a patron.

161.reading: Perunchiththiranar tells Kumanan, who is a height for him and for others as the clouds that gather from the sea fill the Ganga in the hot season, that his wife, sure he has died on the robber-haunted waste a year ago, should be dazed by the wealth of Kumanan's feet, so he asks to ride home on a tall tusked elephant with face-plate and bells, making kings ashamed, and asks Kumanan to measure him by his own greatness rather than by the bard's skill.
161.nuance: The wife's lament is quoted inside the petition (lines 9 to 12): the size of the gift is set by her belief that he is dead. What he asks for is a spectacle, an elephant to ride home on so that ungiving kings are shamed, and the closing turn (do not measure me, measure yourself) puts the burden of worth on the giver.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard driven by want asks a chief for a gift

comparisons.tenor: Kumanan as the height that fills bards and others, as cloud-rain fills the Ganga in the hot season
the massed rain clouds
the elephant's trunk
the strong tusker he asks for

162.reading: Perunchiththiranar tells Ilaveliman that he is not the only patron of suppliants and that patrons are not lacking to them: let him see that askers exist and givers exist; the tall elephant the poet has tied to the guard tree of Ilaveliman's own town, straining it, is the poet's gift, and he is leaving.
162.nuance: Tying an elephant to a chief's guard tree is what a conqueror does to an enemy; the bard does it with an elephant got elsewhere, so the leave-taking is a rebuke. The colophon's other poems by the same poet suggest the elephant was Kumanan's gift, but this poem does not say whose it was.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard takes leave of a patron over the gift

163.reading: The poet tells his wife to give the wealth that Kumanan of the sharp spear, lord of Muthiram where fruit hangs heavy, has granted to everyone, to those who love her and those she loves, to her kin of manifold virtue and to those who lent to ease the family's hunger, without asking whom to favour, without consulting him and without thinking of saving to live well.
163.nuance: The gift begged for the starving household is turned out of the house at once: the bard's wife becomes a giver in her own right, and the poem ends by naming the patron, so the redistribution itself is the praise. நெடுங்குறி எதிர்ப்பை (line 4) seems to mean a loan given on a long promise of return; யாழ in line 3 is a particle, not the lute.

thinai_evidence.note: the patron's gift is named and praised through its giving away

164.reading: Perunthalai Saththanar tells Kumanan that, seeing his hearth so long unused that mushrooms bloom in it, his son crying at each suck of a breast shrivelled and dry from hunger, and his wife's rain-dark eyes brimming, he has come to him, and that now Kumanan knows his state he will not rest without pressing his claim on him, born of a clan that ends the want of drummers and lute players.
164.nuance: The petition is made of the body: the cold hearth, the dry breast with its closed ducts, the wife's tears. The last lines ground the claim not on Kumanan's mood but on his lineage, which is bound to end the want of performers, so the bard asks as of right and says he will hold the patron to it.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard presses a patron for a gift

165.reading: Those who wished to last in an unlasting world set up their fame and died, and the very rich who give nothing to the needy are not remembered like the men of old; the poet sang a lord whose elephants never failed singers, and he, saying that a singer going home empty would grieve him more than the loss of his country, gave the poet his sword so that he might take his head, having nothing dearer than himself; with that triumph the poet now comes, having seen the addressee's kinsman of unretreating resolve.
165.nuance: The argument runs from a maxim (only fame lasts) through its negative (the ungiving rich are forgotten) to the extreme case, a giver who has lost his land and offers his own head. The closing joy is addressed to the giver's kinsman, for whom that head has a price; the poem names neither man, and the story that the kinsman is the brother who drove Kumanan out comes from the colophon tradition, not the verse.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard reports the gift he received

166.reading: Avur Mulankizhar praises Vinnanthayan, descendant of learned men who, keeping to the word of the ancient matted-haired First One, mastered the one old book of four parts and six limbs, broke the pride of disputants by telling false that looks true from truth, and completed the twenty-one sacrifices; wearing the black-buck skin for the rite, with his wives of chaste conduct doing their parts, he has poured ghee more than water, made sacrifices past counting and spread his fame wider than the earth; the poet wishes always to see him so, receiving guests, and says he will go home to his town on the Kaveri to eat and enjoy, while the brahmin should stand on earth like the bamboo-grown Himalaya.
166.nuance: The victory in this vaakai is not in war: it lies in debate and in the count of sacrifices, and the poem counts in riddles (one aim, four, six, three times seven). The bard's closing wish to go home and eat makes the sacrificer a patron like any chief. Several phrases (அறம் புகழ்ந்த வலை சூடி, துணைத் துணைவியர்) are obscure to me.

thinai_evidence.note: the brahmin's excellence in learning and sacrifice is the deed praised

comparisons.tenor: the disputants' false arguments that look like truth
the brahmin, wished to stand long and firm on earth

167.reading: The poet tells Killi of the swift horse that, since he stands against the enemy's army and wins, his sword-scarred body is sweet to hear of and harsh to see, while his enemies, who turn their backs at the sight of him, have unhurt bodies sweet to see and harsh to hear of; each is sweet in one way, so what is there to marvel at in him that the world marvels so?
167.nuance: The praise is a riddle in the senses: the king's wounds belong to the ear (fame), the enemies' whole skins to the eye, and the closing question pretends there is nothing to wonder at when the whole poem has just said what it is.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's victories and wounds are the deed praised

168.reading: On the slopes of Kotran's hill, where boars dig up kanthal tubers and the kuravar sow millet in the turned earth without ploughing, then cook the first new grain with wild-cow milk and venison in an unwashed pot over sandalwood and share it on banana leaves in yards fragrant with wild jasmine, the bards, it is said, praise this lord of the unridden horse, chief of bowmen with vengai garlands and generous hands, every day across the Tamil land, so that his unfading fame shames kings who do not give.
168.nuance: The long kurinji scene praises before the chief is named: a land that feeds without the plough and a meal shared on leaves are the image of his giving. ஊராக் குதிரை, the horse no one rides, reads as the name of his hill (Kuthirai), a riddle on his title.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a giver's fame among bards

169.reading: Since, when your army advances, you are in its van, and when the enemy comes, you hold the rear of your army like a hill across a wide river, the poet tells the chief, a moment of your leisure is always hard to find, but my family's distress is great, so give the gift now; and may your strength, unshaken by foes like the great murukku post at which the young Kosar of victorious spears practise their throws, live long.
169.nuance: The praise is also the excuse: because the chief is always at the front or the rear of battle, the bard cannot wait for the proper moment (செவ்வி) and asks at once. The Kosar's target post makes his strength something that takes every blow and does not fall.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard presses for his gift

comparisons.tenor: the chief holding his army's rear
the chief's strength, struck by foes and unshaken

170.reading: The poet warns the enemy to keep clear of Pittan of the sharp spear, lord of a hill country of little villages with gooseberry fences stripped by wild cows and pebbled yards, where among bowmen who live by the bow the drum of the low-born drummer, struck till his dark hand reddens, echoes the owl in tiger-haunted heights; he gives the dancing women pearls from elephants' tusks and feeds the bards strong toddy, gentle to those who long for him, but to his foes he is like the anvil stone that takes the blows of the dark-handed smith's hammer.
170.nuance: The simile turns on the anvil: what bears the hammer is what shapes the iron, so the enemy who strikes him breaks himself. The poem names the drummer by his low birth (இழிபிறப்பாளன்), a rare plain statement of rank in the hill village.

thinai_evidence.note: a warning to enemies about a chief's strength

comparisons.tenor: Pittan as his enemies meet him

171.reading: Whether we go today, after a short while, or day after day, Kotran gives, never saying he gave before, and fills our empty vessels as we wish; may he finish the hard work his overlord wants; whether one asks for herds of fierce bulls with their stalls, heaps of threshed paddy or jewels with elephants, he gives, and gives to others as well; so may not even a thorn hurt the sole of our lord's foot, and in this world where givers are rare may his feet live so that those who live may live.
171.nuance: The giver is measured by repetition: going daily and being met as on the first day. The wish that his overlord's work be done ties the bards' gifts to the chief's service of his king.

thinai_evidence.note: a chief's habitual giving is described and blessed

172.reading: Set the pot on the fire, cook the rice, see the toddy does not run short, let the dancing women with bright jewels put on garlands, do all such things without worrying about the next meal, for Pittan of the strong horses lives, lord of the hard country where the fire set to guard the hill paddy dies down and bright gems drive off the thick dark; may his spear that wins hard battles, the great giving of his overlord Kothai, and even the hostile kings live long.
172.nuance: The blessing takes in the enemy kings: while they live, Pittan has wars to win and spoils to give, so the feast in the first lines depends on them.

thinai_evidence.note: the bards' household feasts on the strength of a giver

173.reading: May Pannan live as many days as I live; bards, see the trouble of his household: the noise of eating sounds like birds clamouring in a fruiting tree, and children of his large kin go about with rice in their hands like the thin line of tiny ants that carry their eggs to high ground before sure rain; we see it, and yet we ask again and again: is the house of the physician of hunger near or far? Tell us.
173.nuance: The speaker is a Chola king who wishes his own years on a small-village chief and plays a lost suppliant asking the way; the question is feigned, since the crowds with rice in hand already show the road. The hardship (இடும்பை) of the household is its press of guests.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a chief as the healer of hunger

comparisons.tenor: the noise of eating at Pannan's house
the children walking with rice in hand
Pannan, who cures hunger

174.reading: As the god of dark hue brought back the sun when the asuras hid it and the world lay in darkness, so, when the rich Kaveri country had lost its king, the chief showed the moon-white umbrella of the great Valavan, who had stayed in the hard refuge on Mullur, the hill truthful-tongued Kapilan sang, and set it up anew; and now that his famed elder has gone to the world above to enjoy the good he did here, he has appeared to end the grief of hearts searching every road, like thunder-rain that pours after a long summer has cracked the stones, scorched the forest and dried the ponds.
174.nuance: The poem cites an earlier poem: Mullur is the hill Kapilan sang, so the chief's house carries a fame already made in verse. Both similes (the sun restored, rain after drought) are about restoring what was lost, once for the Chola kingdom, once for the chief's own people.

thinai_evidence.note: the deed praised is restoring a king's umbrella

comparisons.tenor: the chief who restored the Chola king
the Valavan's white umbrella
the chief's coming, ending his people's grief

175.reading: My lord Athanungan, those who open my heart will find you there; if ever I forget you, it will be when I forget myself, when life leaves my body, you who every day take up the protection of many, like the wide sun's orb that stands at the rock pass the Moriyar, with their sky-touching umbrellas and bannered chariots, cut for the wheels of their chariots to roll through.
175.nuance: Gratitude is made bodily (open my heart and you are there) and is bounded by life itself, not by any later birth. The Mauryan road cut through the rock serves as a figure for what stays fixed and open to all.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron who protects many

comparisons.tenor: Athanungan, who daily protects many

176.reading: Blessed be the fate that joined me to Nalliyakkodan, lord of great Ilangai with its loud sluices, where girls at play scratching the mud a boar has ploughed find a turtle's rank-smelling eggs with honey-scented lily roots, a giver to those who lack even a small lute; my heart grieves for the days I let pass without seeing him, like people who scorned the cool clear springs of Pari's Parambu because they were in their own town, and thinks of him each time it sees his gentle nature.
176.nuance: The regret is for a giver who was always near: the springs of Parambu were proverbial for never failing, and their very constancy is why those beside them did not value them.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron of bards

comparisons.tenor: the poet, who let days pass without seeing a patron close at hand

177.reading: The gold-decked elephant a bard wins by singing, after waiting many lean days at the bright towns of sword-bearing kings, is not worth as much as the meal at great dawn in the Kudanadu of Athi, whose men, tired of sour kalaa and thudari berries, climb the river's sandbank to pick black jambu fruit, and who, among clustered little forts that let in all who are friends and not even the moonlight if foes, has the white rice thick with the fat of porcupine meat brought by the Eyinar poured without stint for all comers, eaten from big palm-leaf cups.
177.nuance: The comparison runs against the bard's own trade: the king's elephant, won after waiting and hunger, is worth less than a hill chief's rice given at once to anyone who comes. The forts that open to friends and shut even the moon to foes give his hospitality its edge.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a chief's open table

comparisons.tenor: Athi's dawn meal, ranked above a king's gift

178.reading: Saththan of great name, in whose sanded yard elephants weary of the post sigh and horses tire of the stable, swears an oath with the worthy who enter and begs them to eat even when they will not; but he is not only gentle here: in the fearful battle where the weapons of foes are tangled, when the little men who made tall boasts in their own villages with cups of toddy forget them and run in fear, he goes forward and becomes their shelter.
178.nuance: The poem sets the oath he swears to make guests eat beside the boasts the toddy drinkers forget: one man's word at home is kept in battle, the others' is not.

thinai_evidence.note: a man's valour in covering the fleeing

179.reading: When the generous of the earth had died and my begging bowl lay upturned, unfilled, I asked who would fill it, and many named Nagan, lord of Nalai, the soldier of the Pandya who took many lands with tight-strung drums: where an army is wanted he gives his sword, where counsel is wanted his wisdom, a manly heart that never tires under the yoke of what his king wants, of unbeaten fame, whose good battles end the kites' hunger.
179.nuance: The poem is shaped as a bard's search for a giver, with the praise of the soldier given as the answer others offered; the colophon files it under valour, but its frame is the upturned begging bowl.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem's act is a bard asking who will fill his bowl

comparisons.tenor: his service to the king

180.reading: He has no wealth to give without end, nor the meanness to refuse saying he has none; bearing his king's troubles, the wounds that tasted iron in battle have healed and his body is so crossed with sword scars, like a tree cut again and again for medicine, that it is shaped of scars; he lives at Eernthai, enemy of the bards' hunger: old-tongued suppliant, if you want your want ended, come with us, for when we ask him he points to our unfed bellies and asks the dark-handed smith of his town to forge him a long leaf-bladed spear.
180.nuance: The patron is poor, and his gift is a raid: the bards' hunger is shown to the smith, not to a treasury. The scars and the spear make giving the direct fruit of fighting.

thinai_evidence.note: one bard guides another to a giver

comparisons.tenor: his scar-covered body
Maran, the enemy of the bards' hunger

links.note: In 161 Perunchiththiranar asks Kumanan for a tusker to ride home on so that ungiving kings are shamed; in 162 the same poet ties an elephant to Ilaveliman's guard tree and leaves, saying givers exist elsewhere.
links.teaches: Read together, the two poems show the gift elephant doing what 161 promised: the bard's reward from one patron becomes a public rebuke staked at the door of a patron who failed him, so giving among chiefs was a contest the bards could stage.

links.note: 162 says to Ilaveliman: see that askers exist and that givers exist; Kural 1055 says askers stand before others because there are people in the world who do not withhold.
links.teaches: The Kural explains asking by the existence of givers in general; 162 uses that same general truth as a weapon against one particular chief, so the principle that kept the asker's dignity also let him walk away from a mean patron.

links.note: In 159 the poet pictures his wife boiling unsalted greens and his starving household as the reason for his plea to Kumanan; in 163 he tells her to give Kumanan's gift away to all, without consulting him.
links.teaches: The household whose hunger was the bard's argument for the gift becomes, as soon as the gift arrives, a giver to its own kin and creditors, so the bard's reward was expected to circulate, not to be saved.

links.note: Both petitions to Kumanan picture the bard's child sucking a breast dry for want of food (160 lines 17 to 19; 164 lines 3 to 5).
links.teaches: Two different poets press Kumanan with the same picture of the child at the milkless breast, which shows it was a set argument of the plea for a gift (பரிசில் கடாநிலை) rather than one poet's private report.

links.note: 160 shows Kumanan at Muthiram flinging away gold vessels so the bards' troupe may not fail; 165 shows a giver who has lost his land offering his own head because a disappointed bard is worse to him than that loss.
links.teaches: Set beside 160's lavish lord in his own hill, 165 tests the same habit of giving after the land is gone: what remains to give is the self, so the giver's fame survives his loss of wealth.

links.note: Kural 230 says death is the bitterest thing, yet sweet when one cannot give; in 165 the giver says a bard going away disappointed is worse than losing his country and gives his head.
links.teaches: The Kural's ranking of giving above life is a figure of speech in a couplet; 165 gives it a narrative in which a dispossessed chief literally prefers death to failing a bard, so the maxim had a heroic story behind it.

links.note: 165 opens: those who wished to last in an unlasting world set up their fame and died; Kural 233 says nothing in the world stands undying except towering fame.
links.teaches: The Kural states the rule abstractly; 165 places it as the premise of a gift poem and adds its converse, that the ungiving rich are forgotten, so fame here is something the bard both records and withholds.

links.note: Kural 776 makes the day without a noble wound a wasted day; 167 grants the king's scars are sweet to hear of but says they are harsh to see, and the enemies' whole skins sweet to see.
links.teaches: Where the Kural counts the wound only as the warrior's own ledger of worth, 167 adds the onlooker's split response, so the wound's value lies in report and fame, not in how it looks.

links.note: Both name the Kosar of many spears: in Akananuru 113 as loyal guards whose rich land stands for the heroine's lover, in 169 as young men practising spear throws at a murukku post, the simile for Pittan's strength.
links.teaches: The Kosar were a byword for spear-skill and fidelity known to both genres: the akam poet borrows their loyalty to measure a lover's land, the puram poet their training post to measure a chief, so their fame served as a ready image in both kinds of poem.

links.note: Both poems bring in the dark-handed smith (கருங்கைக் கொல்லன்): in 170 the anvil that takes his hammer is the chief facing his foes; in 180 the poor chief asks his town's smith to forge a spear to feed the bards.
links.teaches: The smith's forge stands in both poems for the link between fighting and giving: 170 makes the chief the anvil that wears out his enemies, and 180 shows the spear made there as the source of the bards' meal.

links.note: Kural 227 calls hunger a fierce disease (பசியென்னும் தீப்பிணி) that will not touch one who shares food; 173 calls Pannan the physician of the disease of hunger (பசிப்பிணி மருத்துவன்).
links.teaches: Both books treat hunger as a disease, but the Kural says sharing protects the sharer while 173 makes the giver the healer of other people's hunger, so the image moves from the giver's safety to the hungry crowd's cure.

links.note: In 70 a bard steering another to Killi Valavan names on the way the village of Pannan the open-handed; in 173 a Chola king, Killi Valavan by the colophon, wishes his own years on Pannan and calls him the physician of hunger.
links.teaches: 70 gives Pannan as a landmark of generosity on the road to the king; 173 has a king himself defer to that small-village chief, so Pannan's fame for giving stood in the anthology beside, not beneath, a crowned king's.

links.note: 123 is Kapilar's praise of Malayan, whose gifts outnumber the raindrops on Mullur; 174 refers to Mullur as the hill truthful-tongued Kapilan sang and praises a later chief of the same house.
links.teaches: 174 cites the earlier poem by its poet and place, which shows that a Sangam poet could rest a patron's fame on a famous song already in circulation, and that Mullur's renown was itself made by Kapilar's verse.

links.note: Both use the formula of the Moriyar with sky-touching umbrellas whose chariot wheels cut a pass through rock (Akananuru 69 lines 10 to 12; 175 lines 6 to 8).
links.teaches: The same Mauryan landmark serves akam as the far, dangerous road the hero crosses for wealth and puram as a figure for the fixed, unfailing care of a patron, so the formula's sense came from the poem it was set in, not from the place.

links.note: Kural 107 says one remembers the friendship of those who wiped away one's sorrow for seven births; 175 says the poet will forget Athanungan only when he forgets himself, when life leaves the body.
links.teaches: The Kural stretches gratitude across seven births, while the Purananuru poet bounds it by this one life and locates it in his body, which shows the older poem's gratitude making no claim on rebirth.

links.note: 109 says Parambu's springs are as many as the stars and that it cannot be starved; 176 uses those cool clear springs as what people living beside them did not value.
links.teaches: 109 offers the springs as proof that Pari's hill never fails, and 176 turns that very constancy into a lesson on neglect: what is always at hand, a spring or a near patron, goes unvalued.

links.note: 158 lists the seven great givers who are dead and turns to Kumanan as the one left; 179 opens with the generous of the earth dead and the bard's bowl upturned, and names Nagan of Nalai as the one who will fill it.
links.teaches: After the seven givers died became a reusable opening: 158 applies it to a hill king and 179 to a Pandya's soldier, so a lesser patron could be raised into the line of the great givers by the same formula.

links.note: 167 says the king's sword-scarred body is sweet to hear of and harsh to see; 180 describes a chief whose body is all scars, who has no wealth and gives by having a spear forged.
links.teaches: 167 values the scars as fame; 180 shows them as the price of the bards' meal, since a chief without treasure gives only by fighting, so the wound in puram poetry is both glory and the means of giving.

links.note: Naladiyar 159 says the excellent honour a frequent visitor each time they see him; 171 says Kotran gives whether we come today, later or every day, never saying he gave before.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar states as a mark of character what 171 records of one chief's practice with bards, so the later maxim about the frequent visitor had its model in the patron who gave daily without reproach.

links.note: Naladiyar 100 says the word 'they gave' is heard through the three worlds, further than drum or thunder; 168 says bards praise Kotran across the Tamil land every day, shaming kings who do not give.
links.teaches: 168 shows the mechanism the Naladiyar leaves out: the fame of giving travels because the bards who received the gifts carry it, and it is aimed at the kings who did not give.

new_concepts.gloss: the gift a patron gives a bard or suppliant; also the suppliant who seeks it (பரிசிலர்)
new_concepts.label_source: text: பரிசில் 162 line 6 and 169 line 8; பரிசிலன் 165 line 10; பரிசிலர் 168 line 20

new_concepts.gloss: the guide poem: one who has received a patron's gift directs another seeker to the patron, describing the road and promising the gift
new_concepts.label_source: text: the colophon thurai of 180 (பாணாற்றுப் படையும் ஆம்), and நீயும் வம்மோ? முதுவாய் இரவல in line 9

source_issues: 166: the colophon thurai reads பார்பபன வாகை, a misprint for பார்ப்பன வாகை; copied exactly in colophon and colophon_form, corrected in puram_thurai name.
172 line 5: வெண்டா looks like a misprint for வேண்டா (do not need to); the sense requires the negative.

171 line 13: உற்றாக reads as a wish that the thorn hurt the patron's foot, which contradicts the blessing; the sense needs a negative wish (as if உறாஅற்க), so the line looks corrupt. Marked uncertain.
162 line 5: கடுமரம் is read as கடிமரம், the guarded tree of a chief's town; the spelling may be a variant or a misprint.
163: the review's line table says sangamtamil.com lacks our line 1; line 1 begins the list of those to be given to and is needed by the syntax, so all nine lines are marked.
178: the colophon patron field carries a variant-reading note (பாண்டிக் குதிரைச் சாக்கையன் எனவும் பாடம்) after the name; 179's poet field likewise carries two variant names.
173 line 12 ends with a comma where the poem ends (எமக்கே,).
